slides.title: What do we understand by work?

transcription.tex: Work transfers energy. A force does work when an object moves and the force has a component along the displacement.
For a constant force in the direction of travel, \(W=Fd\). At an angle \(\theta\) to the displacement, \(W=(F\cos\theta)d\).
Directions must be consistent (if not, use components).
Force is measured in newtons and displacement in metres. Work is measured in joules: \(1\,\mathrm J=1\,\mathrm{N\,m}\).
A horizontal force of 8 N moves a box 5 m across a horizontal floor. Calculate the work done by the force.
The force and displacement point in the same direction.\par \(W=Fd=8\times5=40\,\mathrm J\).

slides.title: Work done on a rough slope

transcription.tex: A force \(Y\) moves a particle of mass \(m\) a distance \(x\) up a rough plane inclined at \(30^\circ\). The force acts parallel to the displacement.
The applied force does work \(Yx\). This transfers energy from the source of the force, such as a battery.
Work against friction: \(F_r x\). Friction opposes the motion and transfers energy into heat.
Work against gravity: \((mg\sin30^\circ)x\). Equivalently, multiply the weight \(mg\) by the rise \(x\sin30^\circ\). Both give the same work.
Any remaining work increases kinetic energy if the particle gains speed.\par \(Yx=F_rx+mgx\sin30^\circ+\Delta E_k\).

A package of mass 2 kg is pulled at constant speed for 12 m up a line of greatest slope of a rough plane inclined at \(30^\circ\). The coefficient of friction is 0.35. Calculate:\par (a) the work done against gravity\par (b) the work done against friction\par (c) the total work done by the pulling force.
Constant speed means that kinetic energy does not change.
(a) The vertical rise is \(12\sin30^\circ\). Work against gravity is \(mgh=2g(12\sin30^\circ)=117.6\,\mathrm J\), or 118 J (3 s.f.).
(b) Normal reaction \(R=2g\cos30^\circ\), so \(F_r=0.35R\). Work against friction is \(12(0.35)(2g\cos30^\circ)=71.3\,\mathrm J\) (3 s.f.).

(c) Total work is \(117.6+71.29\ldots=189\,\mathrm J\) (3 s.f.).\par Alternatively, balance forces along the slope: \(P=F_r+2g\sin30^\circ\). Then \(12P=189\,\mathrm J\). The pull must balance both friction and the downslope component of weight.
Question 14

A rough plane surface is inclined at an angle \(\alpha\) to the horizontal, where \(\sin \alpha=\frac{5}{13}\). A packet of mass 8 kg is pulled at a constant speed up a line of greatest slope of the plane. The coefficient of friction between the packet and the plane is 0.3.\par Problem-solving\par Draw a right-angled triangle with sides of length 5, 12 and 13, or use your calculator to find the exact value of \(\cos \alpha.\)\par \textbf{a)} Calculate the magnitude of the frictional force acting on the packet. [5 marks]\par The packet moves a distance of 15 m up the plane. Calculate:\par \textbf{b)} the work done against friction [3 marks]\par \textbf{c)} the work done against gravity. [4 marks]

\(\mu = 0.3\)\par a Resolving perpendicular to the plane:\par \(R = 8g \cos \alpha\) [M1]\par \(= 8g \times \frac{12}{13}\) [A1]\par Friction is limiting:\par \(F = \mu R\) [M1]\par \(F = 0.3 \times 8 \times 9.8 \times \frac{12}{13}\) [A1]\par \(= 21.71\ldots\)\par The frictional force has magnitude \(21.7\,\text{ N}\) (3 s.f.). [A1]
b Work done against friction \(= Fs\) [M1]\par \(= 21.71\ldots \times 15\) [A1]\par \(= 325.6\ldots\)

The work done against friction is \(326\,\text{ J}\) (3 s.f.). [A1]\par c Work done against gravity \(= mgh\) [M1]\par \(= 8 \times 9.8 \times (15 \sin \alpha)\) [M1]\par \(= 8 \times 9.8 \times \left(15 \times \frac{5}{13}\right)\) [A1]\par \(= 452.3\ldots\)\par The work done against gravity is \(452\,\text{ J}\) (3 s.f.) [A1]
Question 15

A rough surface is inclined at an angle \(\arcsin{\frac{7}{25}}\) to the horizontal. A particle of mass 0.5 kg is pulled 3m at a constant speed up the surface by a force acting along a line of greatest slope. The only resistances to the motion are those due to friction and gravity. The work done by the force is 12 J. Calculate the coefficient of friction between the particle and the surface. [5 marks]

Resolving perpendicular to the plane:\par \(R = 0.5g \cos \theta\) [B1]\par \(= 0.5g \times \frac{24}{25}\)\par Resolving parallel to the plane:\par \(T = F + 0.5g \sin \theta\) [M1]\par Friction is limiting:\par \(F = \mu R\) [M1]\par \(F = \mu \times 0.5g \times \frac{24}{25}\)\par \(T = \mu \times 0.5g \times \frac{24}{25} + 0.5g \times \frac{7}{25}\)
Work done by force \(= \text{force} \times \text{distance moved}\)\par \(12 = T \times 3\) [M1]

\(T = 4\)\par \(\therefore 4 = \mu \times 0.5g \times \frac{24}{25} + 0.5g \times \frac{7}{25}\)\par \(\mu = \frac{4 - 0.5 \times 9.8 \times \frac{7}{25}}{0.5 \times 9.8 \times \frac{24}{25}}\)\par \(\mu = 0.5586\dots\)\par The coefficient of friction is 0.559 (3 s.f.) [A1]
Question 16

A rough surface is inclined at \(40^{\circ}\) to the horizontal. A box of mass 1.5 kg is pulled at a constant speed up the surface by a force T acting along a line of greatest slope. The coefficient of friction between the particle and the surface is 0.4. Modelling the box as a particle, calculate the work done by T when the particle travels 8m. [4 marks]

\(\mu=0.4\)\par Resolving perpendicular to the plane:\par \(R=1.5 g \cos 40^{\circ}\)\par Friction is limiting:\par \(F=\mu R\)\par \(F=0.4 \times 1.5 g \cos 40^{\circ}\) [M1]\par Resolving parallel to the plane:\par \(T=F+1.5 g \sin 40^{\circ}\) [M1]\par \(T=0.4 \times 1.5 g \cos 40^{\circ}+1.5 g \sin 40^{\circ}\)\par Work done by \(T=T \times s\)
\(=(0.4 \times 1.5 g \cos 40^{\circ}+1.5 g \sin 40^{\circ}) \times 8\) [M1]\par \(=111.6 \dots\)
The work done by \(T\) is 112 J (3 s.f.) [A1]
Question 17

A particle P of mass 2 kg is projected up a line of greatest slope of a rough plane which is inclined at an angle \(\arcsin\frac{3}{5}\) to the horizontal. The coefficient of friction between P and the plane is 0.35.\par The particle comes to instantaneous rest a distance 3m up the line of greatest slope of the plane. Find:\par \textbf{a)} the work done by gravity [3 marks]\par \textbf{b)} the work done by friction [3 marks]\par \textbf{c)} the speed of projection. [4 marks]

\(\sin \alpha=\frac{3}{5}\Rightarrow\cos \alpha=\frac{4}{5}\)\par Work done equals force multiplied by the distance moved in the direction of the force.\par \textbf{a)} Gravity acts downwards while the particle gains height, so its work is \(W_g=-mgh\). [M1]\par Weight, \(W=mg=2g\), \(h=3\sin\alpha=\frac{9}{5}\) m [A1]\par \(W_g=-2g\times 9/5\).\par \(W_g=-2\times9.8\times1.8=-35.28\;\mathrm J\).

Gravity does −35.3 J of work (3 s.f.). The gravitational potential energy increases by 35.3 J. [A1]\par \textbf{b)} Friction opposes the displacement, so \(W_F=-Fs\), where \(s=3\;\mathrm m\).\par Normal reaction force, \(R\), can be found by resolving perpendicular to the slope:
\(R=2g\cos\alpha\) [M1]\par \(R=\frac{8}{5}g\)

So frictional force, \(F=\frac{7}{20}\times\frac{8}{5}g=\frac{14}{25}g\) [M1]\par \(W_F=-\frac{14}{25}g\times 3\).\par \(W_F=-0.56\times9.8\times3=-16.464\;\mathrm J\).\par Friction does −16.5 J of work (3 s.f.). [A1]\par \textbf{c)} Work done against these forces = kinetic energy lost kinetic energy \(=\frac{1}{2}mv^{2}\) so here: [M1]\par \(35.28+16.464=\left(\frac{1}{2}\times 2u^{2}\right)-\left(\frac{1}{2}\times 2\times 0^{2}\right)\) [M1] [A1]\par \(51.744=u^{2}\)\par \(u=7.1933\ldots\), so the speed of projection is \(7.19\;\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\) (3 s.f.). [A1]
An object of mass \(m\) moving at speed \(v\) has kinetic energy\[E_k=\tfrac12mv^2.\]
For constant acceleration, \(F=ma\) and \(v^2=u^2+2as\). Thus \(Fs=mas=\tfrac12m(v^2-u^2)\). Starting from rest gives \(E_k=\tfrac12mv^2\).
For variable acceleration, \(a=v\,dv/dx\). Hence\[\int F\,dx=\int ma\,dx=\int mv\,dv\]\[=\tfrac12mv^2+C.\] Choose zero kinetic energy at rest, so \(C=0\).
In a uniform gravitational field the potential energy at height \(h\) above a chosen zero level is\[E_p=mgh.\]
Work against gravity equals the gain in potential energy: \(\Delta E_p=mg(h_2-h_1)\). Set \(h_1=0\) to obtain \(mgh\). The symbol \(\Delta\) means “change in”.
Energy and work are measured in joules (J). Use speed, the magnitude of velocity, in the kinetic energy formula. The expression \(mgh\) assumes constant \(g\).

parts.text: Fill in the gaps in the table below

transcription.tex: A parcel of mass 3 kg is pulled 10 m up a line of greatest slope of a plane, where \(\tan\theta=3/4\).\par (a) Calculate the potential energy gained.\par (b) What speed would the parcel acquire if all this energy were transferred into kinetic energy?
(a) The 3–4–5 triangle gives \(\sin\theta=3/5\). The height gained is \(10\sin\theta=6\,\mathrm m\).\par \(\Delta E_p=3(9.8)(6)=176.4\,\mathrm J\), or 176 J (3 s.f.).
Round the final answers to an appropriate precision. Use the unrounded 176.4 J in part (b) to avoid intermediate rounding error.

A small package P is modelled as a particle of mass 0.6 kg. The package slides down a rough plane from a point S to a point T, where \(ST=12 \mathrm{m}\). The plane is inclined at an angle of \(30^{\circ}\) to the horizontal and \(ST\) is a line of greatest slope of the plane, as shown in Figure 3. The speed of P at S is \(10 \mathrm{m} \mathrm{s}^{-1}\) and the speed of P at T is \(9 \mathrm{m} \mathrm{s}^{-1}\).\par (a) Calculate the total loss of energy of P in moving from S to T,\par (b) Given that the work done against friction by P is equal to total loss of energy of P in moving from S to T, calculate the coefficient of friction between P and the plane.
Figure 3
(a) Kinetic energy lost: \(\tfrac12(0.6)(10^2-9^2)=5.7\,\mathrm J\). Potential energy lost: \(0.6(9.8)(12\sin30^\circ)=35.28\,\mathrm J\). Total loss: \(40.98\,\mathrm J\), or 41.0 J (3 s.f.).
(b) Normal reaction \(R=0.6(9.8)\cos30^\circ=5.09\ldots\,\mathrm N\). Work against friction is \(12\mu R=40.98\). Therefore \(\mu=40.98/[12(0.6)(9.8)\cos30^\circ]=0.671\) (3 s.f.).
Question 7

A playground slide is modelled as a plane inclined at \(48^{\circ}\) to the horizontal. A child of mass 25 kg slides down the slide for 4 m.\par \textbf{a)} Calculate the potential energy lost by the child. [4 marks]\par \textbf{b)} State one assumption that you have made in your calculations, and comment on its validity. [1 mark]

P.E. lost \(= mgh\) [M1]\par \(= 25 \times 9.8 \times(4 \sin 48^{\circ})\) [M1]\par \(= 728.2 \dots\) [A1]\par The P.E. lost by the child is 728 J (3 s.f.) [A1]\par \textbf{b)} Model the child as a particle whose centre of mass descends through the same vertical distance as the slide.\par This is reasonable if the child stays in the same posture. The gravitational potential energy lost depends only on the vertical fall. [B1]
Question 8

A ball of mass 0.6 kg is dropped from a height of 2m into a pond.\par \textbf{a)} Calculate the kinetic energy of the ball as it hits the surface of the water. [3 marks]\par The ball begins to sink in the water with a speed of \(4.8\,\mathrm{m\,s}^{-1}\).\par \textbf{b)} Calculate the kinetic energy lost when the ball strikes the water. [4 marks]

\textbf{a)} \(s=2\,\mathrm{~m}, a=9.8\,\mathrm{~m}\,\mathrm{s}^{-2}, u=0, v=?\)\par \(v^{2}=u^{2}+2 a s\) [M1]\par \(v^{2}=0+2 \times 9.8 \times 2\)\par \(v^{2}=39.2\)\par K.E. \(=\frac{1}{2} m v^{2}=\frac{1}{2} \times 0.6 \times 39.2\) [M1]\par \(=11.76\)\par The K.E. of the ball as it hits the surface of the water is 11.8 J (3 s.f.) [A1]\par \textbf{b)} K.E. lost \(=\frac{1}{2} m u^{2}-\frac{1}{2} m v^{2}\) [M1]\par \(=11.76-\frac{1}{2} \times 0.6 \times 4.8^{2}\) [M1] [A1]\par \(=4.848\)\par The K.E. lost by the ball is 4.85 J (3 s.f.) [A1]
Question 10

A car of mass 750 kg moves along a stretch of road which can be modelled as a line of greatest slope of a plane inclined to the horizontal at \(30^{\circ}\). As the car moves up the road for 500m its speed reduces from \(20\,\mathrm{m\,s}^{-1}\) to \(15\,\mathrm{m\,s}^{-1}\). Calculate:\par \textbf{a)} the loss of kinetic energy of the car [3 marks]\par \textbf{b)} the gain of potential energy of the car. [4 marks]

\(\mathrm{K.E.}=\frac{1}{2} m u^{2}-\frac{1}{2} m v^{2}\) [M1]\par \(=\frac{1}{2}\times 750 \times 20^{2}-\frac{1}{2}\times 750 \times 15^{2}\) [A1]\par \(=65625\)\par The loss of K.E of the car is 65 625 J [A1]\par \textbf{b)} Gain of P.E.=mgh [M1]\par \(=750 \times 9.8 \times(500 \sin 30^{\circ})\) [M1] [A1]\par \(=1837500\)\par The gain of P.E. of the car is 1 837 500 J [A1]
Question 11
A woman of mass 80 kg climbs a vertical cliff face of height h m. Her potential energy increases by 15.7 kJ.\par Find the height of the cliff. [3 marks]
P.E. = mgh [M1]\par \(15.7 \times1000=80 \times9.8 h\) [A1]\par \(h=\frac{15.7 \times1000}{80 \times9.8}\)\par \(h=20.02\)\par The cliff is 20.0 m high (3 s.f.) [A1]
The total energy of an isolated system stays constant. Choose the system and a zero level for gravitational potential energy before comparing its initial and final states.
A driving force transfers energy into the system, for example from a battery or engine. A resistive force transfers mechanical energy into heat and sometimes sound.
Initial energy + work supplied = final energy + work against resistance.\par \(W_{\rm in}+\tfrac12mu^2+mgh_1\)\par \(\qquad=\tfrac12mv^2+mgh_2+W_{\rm out}\).

For constant forces parallel or antiparallel to travel over distance \(s\), use \(W_{\rm in}=F_{\rm drive}s\) and \(W_{\rm out}=F_{\rm resist}s\). This is the work–energy principle applied to the motion.

A particle of mass 2 kg is projected at \(8\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\) up a line of greatest slope on a rough plane inclined at \(45^\circ\). The coefficient of friction is 0.4. Calculate the distance travelled before it comes to instantaneous rest.
The plane exerts a normal reaction perpendicular to the surface. Friction and the component of the weight along the slope both act downhill.
Choose the start as zero potential energy. After projection there is no driving force. At the turning point kinetic energy is zero.
For distance \(x\), the rise is \(h=x\sin45^\circ\). The reaction is \(R=2g\cos45^\circ\), so friction is \(F_r=0.4R\).

Initial kinetic energy = gain in potential energy + work against friction.\par \(\tfrac12(2)(8^2)=2gh+F_rx\)\par \(64=2gx\sin45^\circ+0.4(2g\cos45^\circ)x\).\par \(x=64/[2g(\sin45^\circ+0.4\cos45^\circ)]=3.30\,\mathrm m\) (3 s.f.).

A skier is moving downhill and passes point A on a ski run at \(6\;\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). After descending 50m vertically the run begins to ascend. When the skier has ascended 25m to the point B her speed is \(4\;\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). The skier and her skis have a combined mass of 55kg. The total distance she travels from A to B is 1400m. The non-gravitational resistances to motion are constant and have a total magnitude of 12N. Calculate the work done by the skier.

shapes.alt: Cross-country skier pushing uphill with poles

transcription.tex: Use energy at A + work done by the skier = energy at B + work against resistance. Take the lowest point as zero gravitational potential energy.\par \(W+\tfrac12(55)(6^2)+55(9.8)(50)=\tfrac12(55)(4^2)+55(9.8)(25)+12(1400)\).\par \(W=2780\;\mathrm J\) (3 s.f.).
Tip: Gravity supplies energy on the descent. The skier can also do work by pushing with the poles, as shown in the second photograph.

Two particles A and B, of mass m and 2m respectively, are attached to the ends of a light inextensible string. The particle A lies on a rough plane inclined at an angle \(\alpha\) to the horizontal, where \(\tan \alpha=\frac{3}{4}\). The string passes over a small light smooth pulley P fixed at the top of the plane. The particle B hangs freely below P, as shown in Figure 2. The particles are released from rest with the string taut and the section of the string from A to P parallel to a line of greatest slope of the plane. The coefficient of friction between A and the plane is \(\frac{5}{8}\). When each particle has moved a distance h, B has not reached the ground and A has not reached P.\par (a) Find an expression for the potential energy lost by the system when each particle has moved a distance h.\par [2 marks]\par When each particle has moved a distance h, they are moving with speed \(v\). Using the work-energy principle,\par (b) find an expression for \(v^{2}\), giving your answer in the form \(kgh\), where k is a number.\par [5 marks]
Figure 2
(a) B loses \(2mgh\) and A gains \(mgh\sin\alpha\). [M1] Since \(\sin\alpha=3/5\), the system loses \(7mgh/5\). [A1]

(b) Normal reaction \(R=mg\cos\alpha=4mg/5\). [B1] Work against friction is \((5/8)Rh=mgh/2\). [M1] Equate the energy lost to work and the kinetic energy gained: \(\tfrac12mv^2+\tfrac12(2m)v^2=7mgh/5-mgh/2\). [A1] Thus \(3mv^2/2=9mgh/10\) [A1] and \(v^2=3gh/5\). [A1]

A starts on the rough plane and B starts a distance \(s\) above the ground. Find the total distance travelled by A before it first comes to rest. Use \(\tan\alpha=3/4\), \(\mu=5/8\) and \(v^2=3gs/5\) when B reaches the ground.
The alternative balance for the connected system is \(0=\tfrac12mv^2+\tfrac12(2m)v^2+mgh\sin\alpha-2mgh+\mu Rh\).

Let \(x\) be A’s extra distance after B reaches the ground. The string goes slack. Gravity and friction slow A.\par \(\tfrac12mv^2=mgx\sin\alpha+\mu mgx\cos\alpha\).\par Substitute \(v^2=3gs/5\), \(\sin\alpha=3/5\) and \(\cos\alpha=4/5\):\par \(3s/10=3x/5+(5/8)(4/5)x=11x/10\).\par Thus \(x=3s/11\). Adding the first distance \(s\) gives a total distance of \(14s/11\).
Question 5

A box of mass 3 kg is projected from point A across a rough horizontal floor with speed \(6\,\mathrm{~m}\,\mathrm{s}^{-1}\) The box moves in a straight line across the floor and comes to rest at point B.The coefficient of friction between the box and the floor is 0.4.\par \textbf{a)} Calculate the kinetic energy lost by the box. [2 marks]\par \textbf{b)} Write down the work done against friction. [1 mark]\par \textbf{c)} Calculate the distance AB. [5 marks]

\(\mu=0.4\)\par \textbf{a)} K.E. lost \(=\frac{1}{2} m u^{2}-\frac{1}{2} m v^{2}\) [M1]\par \(=\frac{1}{2}\times 3\times 6^{2}-0\)\par \(=54\)\par The kinetic energy lost by the box is 54 J [A1]\par \textbf{b)} The work done against friction is 54 J [B1]

\textbf{c)} Resolving perpendicular to the floor: \(R=3 g\) [M1] Friction is limiting: \(F=\mu R\) [M1]\par \(F=0.4 \times3 g\) [M1] Work done \(= F s\)\par \(54=0.4 \times3 g \times s\) [A1]\par \(s=\frac{54}{0.4 \times3 g}=4.591 \dots\) [A1] The distance AB is 4.59 m (3 s.f.)
Question 10

A bullet of mass 150g travelling at \(500\,\mathrm{m\,s}^{-1}\) horizontally hits a vertical wall. The resistive force exerted by the wall on the bullet is modelled as having a constant magnitude of 250000 N.\par \textbf{a)} Calculate the distance that the bullet penetrates the wall. [4 marks]\par \textbf{b)} State how the model for the resistive force could be refined to make it more realistic. [1 mark]

10a Loss of K.E \(= \frac{1}{2} m u^{2}-\frac{1}{2} m v^{2}\) [M1]\par \(= \frac{1}{2} \times 0.15 \times 500^{2}-0\) Work done by resistance \(= F s\) [M1]\par \(= 250000 s\) Work done by resistance \(= \mathrm{loss}\) of K.E. \(250000 s=\frac{1}{2} \times 0.15 \times 500^{2}\) [A1]\par \(s=\frac{\frac{1}{2} \times 0.15 \times 500^{2}}{250000}\)\par \(= 0.075\) [A1] The distance the bullet penetrates the wall is 0.075 m (or 75 mm)\par \textbf{b)} The resistive force could depend on the speed of the bullet. [B1]
Question 15

A box of mass 2 kg is projected with speed \(6\,\mathrm{~m}\,\mathrm{s}^{-1}\) up a line of greatest slope of a rough plane inclined at \(30^{\circ}\) to the horizontal. The coefficient of friction between the box and the plane is \(\frac{1}{3}\). Use the work-energy principle to calculate the distance the box travels up the plane before coming to rest. [5 marks]

K.E. lost \(= \frac{1}{2} m u^{2}-\frac{1}{2} m v^{2}\)\par \(= \frac{1}{2} \times 2 \times 6^{2}-0\)\par \(= 36\) [B1]\par P.E. gained \(= m g h\)\par \(= 2 \times 9.8 \times( x \sin 30^{\circ})\)\par \(= 9.8 x\) [M1]\par Resolving perpendicular to the plane: \(R=2 g \cos 30^{\circ}\)\par Friction is limiting: \(F=\mu R\)
\(F=\frac{1}{3} \times 2 g \cos 30^{\circ}=\frac{2}{3} g \cos 30^{\circ}\) [M1]\par Work done against friction \(F x=\frac{2}{3} g x \cos 30^{\circ}\)
K.E. lost \(= P.E.\) gained \(+\) work done against friction

\(\Rightarrow 36=9.8 x+\frac{2}{3} g x \cos 30^{\circ}\) [M1]\par \(36=9.8 x \left( 1+\frac{2}{3} \cos 30^{\circ} \right)\)\par \(x=\frac{36}{9.8 \left( 1+\frac{2}{3} \cos 30^{\circ} \right)}=2.328 \dots\)\par The particle moves 2.33 m up the plane (3 s.f.) [A1]
Question 16

A tennis ball of mass 58 g is hit vertically upwards by a tennis racket from a point 1 metre above the ground. Given that the tennis ball receives an impulse of 1.7 Ns,\par \textbf{a)} find the initial speed of the ball. [3 marks]\par The ball first comes to rest at a point 28 m above the ground.\par \textbf{b)} Find the energy lost due to air resistance by the ball during this motion. [3 marks]\par Given that the air resistance is modelled as a constant force of magnitude RN,\par \textbf{c)} find the value of R. [2 marks]

\textbf{a)} Resolving vertically:\par \(I=mv-mu\) [M1]\par \(1.7=0.058 v-0.058 \times 0\) [A1]\par \(v=\frac{1.7}{0.058}\)\par \(v=29.31 \dots\)\par The initial speed of the ball is \(29.3\,\mathrm{~ m}\,\mathrm{s}^{-1}\) (3 s.f.) [A1]\par \textbf{b)} Subtract the final potential energy from the initial kinetic energy to find the energy lost.\par \(=\frac{1}{2} m v^{2}-m g h\) [M1]
The energy lost due to air resistance is \(9.57\,\mathrm{~ J}\) (3 s.f.) [A1]

\textbf{c)} The work done against air resistance equals the energy lost.\par \(R \times 27=9.566 \dots\) [M1]\par \(R=\frac{9.566 \dots}{27}\)\par \(R=0.354 \dots\)\par The value of \(R\) is \(0.354\) (3 s.f.) [A1]
Question 17

A skier of mass 80 kg skis down a straight hill inclined at \(30^{\circ}\) to the horizontal. The speed of the skier increases from \(3\,\mathrm{m\,s}^{-1}\) to \(12\,\mathrm{m\,s}^{-1}\).\par The total resistances to motion of the skier due to friction and air resistance are modelled as a constant force of magnitude RN.\par \textbf{a)} Given that the skier travels a total distance of 50m, find the value of R. [5 marks]\par \textbf{b)} Suggest one way in which the model could be refined. [1 mark]

\textbf{a)} Work done against resistance equals the loss of mechanical energy.\par Loss in P.E. \(= mgh\)\par Increase in K.E. \(= \frac{1}{2} m v^{2}-\frac{1}{2} m u^{2}\) [M1]\par Total loss of energy \(=\) P.E. lost \(-\) K.E. gained\par \(= mgh+\frac{1}{2} m u^{2}-\frac{1}{2} m v^{2}\) [M1]\par Force \(\times\) distance \(= mgh+\frac{1}{2} m u^{2}-\frac{1}{2} m v^{2}\) [M1]
\(50 R \equiv( 80 \times9.8 \times50 \sin 30^{\circ})+\left( \frac{1}{2} \times80 \times3^{2} \right)-\left( \frac{1}{2} \times80 \times12^{2} \right)\) [A1]

\(50 R=14\ 200\)\par \(R=284\)\par The magnitude of the resistive force is \(284\;\mathrm{N}\). [A1]\par \textbf{b)} Allow the resistive force to depend on speed, for example by modelling air resistance separately from friction at the skis. [B1]
Question 18

A box of mass 70 kg starts at rest and slides in a straight line down a surface inclined at \(20^{\circ}\) to the horizontal. After the box has travelled a distance of 60 m, the surface becomes horizontal, and the box slides a further 50 m before coming to rest. The total resistance due to friction and air resistance is modelled as a force of constant magnitude RN which acts so as to oppose the direction of motion of the box. Find the value of R. [7 marks]

Change in K.E. \(= \frac{1}{2} m v^2 - \frac{1}{2} m u^2\)\par \(= 0 - 0\) [B1]\par Loss of P.E. \(= m g h\) [M1]\par \(= 70 \times 9.8 \times (60 \sin 20^\circ)\) [A1]\par Work done against resistance \(= F s\)\par \(= R \times (60 + 50)\) [M1]\par \(= 110 R\)\par Work done against resistance \(= \text{loss of P.E.}\) [M1]\par \(110 R = 70 \times 9.8 \times (60 \sin 20^\circ)\) [A1]
\(R = \frac{70 \times 9.8 \times 60 \sin 20^\circ}{110}\)\par \(R = 127.9\)
The value of \(R\) is 128 N (3 s.f.) [A1]
Question 19

A girl and her sledge have a combined mass of 40 kg. She starts from rest and descends a slope which is inclined at \(25^{\circ}\) to the horizontal. At the bottom of the slope the ground becomes horizontal for 15m before rising at \(6^{\circ}\) to the horizontal. The girl travels 25m up the slope before coming to rest once more. There is a constant resistance to motion of magnitude 18 N. Calculate the distance the girl travels down the slope initially. [7 marks]

Loss of P.E. \(= mgh\)\par \(= 40 \times 9.8 \times (x \sin 25^{\circ} - 25 \sin 6^{\circ})\) [M1] [A1]\par Change in K.E. \(= \frac{1}{2} m v^{2} - \frac{1}{2} m u^{2}\)\par \(= 0 - 0\) [B1]\par Work done against resistance \(= Fs\)\par \(= 18 \times (x + 15 + 25)\) [M1]\par \(= 18 \times (x + 40)\)\par Work done against resistance \(= \text{loss of P.E.}\) [M1]
\(18x + 18 \times 40 = 40 \times 9.8 \times x \sin 25^{\circ} - 40 \times 9.8 \times 25 \sin 6^{\circ}\)
\((40 \times 9.8 \sin 25^{\circ} - 18)x = 18 \times 40 + 40 \times 9.8 \times 25 \sin 6^{\circ}\) [M1]
\(x = \frac{18 \times 40 + 40 \times 9.8 \times 25 \sin 6^{\circ}}{40 \times 9.8 \sin 25^{\circ} - 18}\)\par \(x = 11.81\ldots\)\par The girl travels \(11.8\,\text{ m}\) down the slope. [A1]
Power is the rate of energy transfer or the rate of doing work.\[P=\frac{dW}{dt}.\]
For a constant force along the displacement, \(W=Fs\). Hence average power is \(Fs/t\). Instantaneously, \(P=F\,ds/dt=Fv\).
For a driving force parallel to the motion, \(F=P/v\) when \(v>0\). For a force at an angle, use the scalar product \(P=\mathbf F\cdot\mathbf v\).
The unit of power is the watt (W).\par \(1\,\mathrm W=1\,\mathrm{J\,s^{-1}}=1\,\mathrm{kg\,m^2\,s^{-3}}\).
An energy balance still includes work over a distance: \(F_{\rm drive}s+\tfrac12mu^2+mgh_1=\tfrac12mv^2+mgh_2+F_{\rm resist}s\).

A van of mass 1250 kg is travelling along a horizontal road. The van’s engine is working at 24 kW. The constant resistance to motion has a magnitude of 600 N. Calculate:\par (a) the acceleration of the van when it is travelling at \(6\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\)\par (b) the maximum speed of the van.

(a) Take the direction of travel as positive. At \(6\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\), use \(P=Tv\).\par \(T=24\,000/6=4000\,\mathrm N\).\par By Newton’s second law, \(T-600=1250a\).\par \(a=(4000-600)/1250=2.72\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\).

(b) At maximum speed the acceleration is zero. The new driving force \(T^{\prime}\) balances the resistance, so \(T^{\prime}=600\,\mathrm N\).\par \(24\,000=600v_{\max}\).\par \(v_{\max}=40\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).

(a) The cyclist travels at constant speed, so the resultant force along the road is zero.
